10387-a-century-too-soon-the-age-of-tyra:
John R. Musick published this historical romance in 1909, as volume six of his Real America in Romance series. Its subject is Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia, a century before American independence, when colonists first stirred against royal rule. Musick calls the age one of tyranny, yet full of early republican feeling.

Cavaliers and Puritans, Quakers and Catholics, divide the colony, while brave, gallant, and sober settlers clash over power and faith. The sleeping goddess of liberty, Musick says, opened her eyes, then slept again for a hundred years. Readers get a vivid, period tale of colonial revolt.
1246-the-house-of-dust-a-symphony:
Conrad Aiken, an American poet, builds this long poem as a symphony in four movements. Voices speak from a house of dust: lovers, dreamers, and the dead, all passing through rooms of memory. The poem moves in waves of image and music rather than in story.

Aiken's lines are lush and dreamlike, full of sea, wind, and light, and the poem's form was bold for its day. It won praise as a landmark of modern American verse. The book suits readers who like poetry that works like music, with mood carrying the sense.
13043-william-of-germany:
William of Germany, by Stanley Shaw, published in 1913, traces Kaiser Wilhelm II from youth through his reign to 1913. Chapters follow his boyhood, the years before he took the throne, the accession of 1888, the court, and the break with Bismarck known as dropping the pilot. Later sections cover Morocco, the November storm of 1908, and the emperor as he stood in 1913.

Bismarck's public replies in the Hamburg News show the clash at the heart of the book, above all over the 1890 deal that gave Germany Heligoland for Zanzibar. Shaw's life of the Kaiser remains a useful early English portrait of a ruler whose choices shaped Europe.
13664-selections-from-the-writings-of-lo:
Selections from Lord Dunsany's writings, 1912, gather The Gods of the Mountain, the first act of King Argimenes and the Unknown Warrior. The Fall of Babbulkund, The Sphinx at Gizeh, Idle Days on the Yann, A Miracle, and The Castle of Time. Lady Wilde's tale of a Dublin crowd opens the book, as a young girl escapes into a shop.

Agmar questions a man who saw gods terrible in the gloaming, green and not as they now appear, while children who saw them died. Travellers journey south through desert to an oasis of palms by a well, watering haughty camels, resting in shade, and singing songs of Babbulkund. Dunsany's prose is dreamlike, ornate, and strange, building whole mythologies in a few pages.
13800-the-pleasures-of-a-single-life-or-:
Printed in London in 1709 for one penny, this satire praises single life and mocks matrimony. It claims occasion from divorces lately granted by Parliament. Verse opens with wedlock as a cursed, uncomfortable state, cause of woes and object of hate. The speaker recalls calm joys before fatal cares oppressed him.

A companion piece, The Choice, praises pleasures of a country life. The satire addresses beaus against the next vacation, urging them to stay free. Its humour is coarse and of its age, with talk of dying convicts torn between fear and reprieve. The pamphlet suits students of Restoration and Augustan satire. It also shows early print culture at street price.
14233-over-strand-and-field-a-record-of-:
Gustave Flaubert's record of travel through Brittany, published in Chicago in 1904, begins at Chambord. Empty galleries and deserted rooms show spiders spinning over Francis the First's salamanders. Poverty here has no grandeur, Flaubert writes: floors repaired in one room rot in the next, in futile effort to preserve what dies. Conscious poverty brushes its threadbare coat and tries to look respectable.

Coast walking follows. Cliffs crowd, pile, and overturn, and travelers slide on slippery rock while a swallow cuts luminous air above them. Bear-baiting supplies a brutal interlude: dogs cling to a bear's back, men bite dogs to loosen jaws, and a mattock frees one bulldog's grip. Dust settles on spectators as beasts gasp and men pull hairs from their teeth. Flaubert's eye stays pitiless and poetic, finding beauty and cruelty side by side on the Breton shore.
14407-the-tale-of-benjamin-bunny:
Beatrix Potter's 1904 picture book brings back Peter Rabbit's cousin Benjamin, who slips into Mr. McGregor's garden to rescue Peter's lost clothes. The tale, written for the children of Sawrey, follows the earlier Peter Rabbit story.

Benjamin and Peter dodge the cat, hide under baskets, and climb down a pear tree into lettuce beds, leaving small footmarks everywhere. Potter's watercolor scenes of garden, wall, and wood carry much of the charm. The book is short, gentle, and funny, and it remains one of the best-loved entries in her animal tales.
15977-frank-and-fanny:
A rural story for children by Mrs. Clara Moreton, issued by Phillips, Sampson and Company in Boston in 1851, entered in 1850. Numerous engravings join the text. Moreton's preface states her purpose plainly: to inculcate gentleness, patience, and benevolence, and to inspire the young with love for simple rural pleasures.

Frank and Fanny live a country childhood of fields, chores, and kind deeds. Exciting narratives, Moreton warns, do not favour the mild virtues, which she calls the most beautiful ornaments of character. Her tale keeps its pace gentle and its lessons clear. The book gives a mid-century ideal of childhood: quiet, good, and happy in the country.
16040-kenny:
Leona Dalrymple's novel Kenny, illustrated by Joseph Pierre Nuyttens and printed in Chicago in 1917, follows a household of strong-willed people in a country setting. Chapter titles trace the action: Brian rebels, a cabin in the pines, a blossom storm, a miser's will and gold, Kenny's truth crusade, and Kenny's ward. Joan, Adam Craig, and a chair by the fire all take their place in the story.

The book mixes family quarrels, romance, and mystery with a warm, outdoor feeling, moving from spring weather to a shadow of death and back toward hope. Dalrymple, known for Diane of the Green Van, writes lively, popular fiction for general readers. Kenny offers a pleasant, old-fashioned tale of youth, pride, and second chances.
1646-roads-of-destiny:
O. Henry gathers short stories around chance and choice. The small turn that changes a life drives the title tale, following a young shepherd who leaves home after a quarrel and faces three different roads. The collection moves between Texas ranches, city rooms, and village streets, and its people are clerks, cowboys, lovers, and drifters.

What holds the stories together is O. Henry's trick of the late reversal: a plan collapses, a stranger proves to be someone else, or a kindness lands where it was least expected. Readers who like plot-driven tales with a sting in the last page will find the author's best-known manner here, in short, self-contained form.
16779-a-ryght-profytable-treatyse-compen:
Thomas Betson wrote this short profitable treatise, drawn from many writings of holy men, printed in Caxton's house by Wynkyn de Worde about 1500 and reprinted at Cambridge University Press in 1905. It is one of twenty-six tracts once bound together in a volume given to Cambridge in 1715 by King George I with Bishop John Moore's library. Betson's name comes only from the colophon.

The treatise gathers short counsels for a devout life, in the plain, pious style of late medieval England. Its reprint keeps old spelling and marks for modern readers. The book gives a rare glimpse of what ordinary holy folk read around 1500, short, practical, and meant for daily use rather than for scholars.
17141-destiny:
Charles Neville Buck's 1916 novel opens in a White Mountains schoolhouse, where a slight thirteen-year-old boy broods apart from his mates. Part One, called The Land of Promise, follows his youth, his dreams, and the pull of a wider life beyond the hills. Autumn maples, chestnuts, and schoolroom drones set a vivid, almost dreamy scene for his start.

Buck writes in rich, romantic prose, with fate and choice as twin threads through the hero's growth. The book suits readers who like old-style tales of a poor boy, a hard start, and a life shaped by will and chance. Its first part alone gives a full sense of the boy, his place, and his hopes.
17928-the-influence-of-india-and-persia-:
Arthur F. J. Remy wrote The Influence of India and Persia on the Poetry of Germany in 1901, printed by Columbia University Press in New York. Remy, a fellow in comparative philology at Columbia, dedicates the study to his teachers William Carpenter and Calvin Thomas.

Chapters trace what medieval Europe knew of India and Persia, then follow Portuguese voyages, Persian studies, and the slow arrival of Indian lore in German letters. Remy shows how Eastern tales, images, and faiths seeped into German verse. The book is a learned, early study of East-West letters, still useful for students of that rich exchange.
18632-crossroads-of-destiny:
H. Beam Piper wrote this short story for Fantastic Universe in July 1959. Its narrator, a college history teacher, keeps a dollar bill in his bank box as proof of a strange night, afraid to show it even to fellow teachers. In a train club car he hears five men debate how history might shift if Columbus had sailed under the English flag of Henry VII rather than Spain.

One of the men takes notes for a planning staff, hinting the talk is more than idle fancy. Piper plays the what-if with a straight face, letting small choices loom large. The story is a neat early example of alternate-history fiction, short, sly, and easy to read in one sitting.
18948-damn-a-book-of-calumny:
H. L. Mencken published this short book in New York in 1918, in a third printing from Philip Goodman Company. It is a string of brief, sharp pieces on subjects that run from patriotism and art to humor, lying, war, actors, clubs, and marriage. Each item runs only a page or two, and the table of contents reads like a list of targets.

Mencken's method is attack by aphorism: a bold claim, a quick example, and a sting in the tail. He mocks moral indignation, praises the artist against the crowd, and doubts most respectable opinion. Readers get Mencken at his most combative and quotable, a good short introduction to the critic who shaped American newspaper wit in the 1920s.
19017-tales-of-destiny:
Edmund Mitchell wrote this 1913 book of tales told by Indian narrators, from a Rajput chief to a fakir, a merchant, and an Afghan general. Each tale turns on fate, stars, or a vow, and each teller speaks in his own voice. The frame is a circle of storytellers in Mughal India.

One tale follows Rukpur Singh, chief of Jhalnagor and captain of Akbar's guard, into battle with elephants, matchlocks, and falling rocks. Others deal with diamonds, tigers, and a mother's love. Readers get rich, old-style Eastern tales where destiny rules and courage meets its price.
19565-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-and:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book about Bunny Brown, his sister Sue, and their Shetland pony; its New York printing appeared in the late nineteen teens with pictures by Thelma Gooch. It belongs to a long series that took the pair to farms, circuses, camps, and city homes.

Here Toby the pony carries them over a ford on a smooth gravel bed, then clattering back over a bridge, while the children talk over their good time. The book's simple pleasures, animals, water, and roads, made it a steady favorite with young readers.
2023-malvina-of-brittany:
Jerome K. Jerome collects short comic stories here, led by the title tale of Malvina of Brittany, a strange visitor whose coming unsettles a quiet household. A doctor who doubts the story still admits it changed how he sees life. Jerome wrote these stories between his famous comic novels, keeping the same easy voice for shorter work.

Other pieces include a street with a blank wall, an evening out, a lesson, and a pair of fawn gloves, each told with Jerome's dry humor. The tales mix the everyday with a touch of the uncanny, and none takes itself too seriously. The uncanny touches stay light, since Jerome prefers a laugh to a chill, and his ghosts seldom mean real harm.
21304-begumbagh-a-tale-of-the-indian-mut:
George Manville Fenn fills this volume with a long tale and three shorter stories. It starts with Begumbagh, about a small British garrison holding out during the Indian Mutiny. A one-armed narrator tells it, holding his sliding paper down with a lead inkstand. Suspense, Fenn's trademark, drives every chapter.

The second story concerns cursed gold plate in an old gentleman's house, and the curse proves real. The third traps two smugglers in a gowt, a sea drain cut in eastern England. The last follows a fine new ship through an Atlantic storm after her captain takes to drink and a junior officer takes command.
22319-mezzerow-loves-company:
Mezzerow Loves Company is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its scene opens with a welcome to Earth. An official greets newcomers arriving from the outer worlds.

He can spot fresh arrivals by one small sign. Their eyes lack the identifying gleam that marks everyone else. On principle, he would stamp one woman's passport with dull and dingy ink. That petty detail gives the future world its bureaucratic chill. The story builds its strange society out of stamps, eyes, and quiet dread. Readers meet a compact tale about belonging, papers, and being marked as an outsider on sight.
22774-barbara-in-brittany:
Barbara in Brittany is a children's story of an English girl's stay in Brittany, the Celtic corner of France. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Travel tales for girls of the era mixed mild adventure with lessons in foreign custom, and Brittany, with its pardons, costumes, and coast, was a favorite ground.

The sample catches a small moral moment: Barbara holds little Lucy in her lap and coaxes her out of shyness. You won't run off the moment she speaks to you, will you, Lucy? It's rude, you know. Try to answer nicely when she wants you to. French hosts, strange food, and new friends presumably test both girls further. The book offers a gentle tour of Brittany through a child's eyes, manners included.
23500-the-car-of-destiny:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote this nineteen hundred seven Spanish romance, dedicated to Dona Maria del Pilar Harvey and pictured by Armand Both. Lady Monica, the heroine, moves through a tale of a king's car, a guest who was not asked, a mystery over a chauffeur, and a chase over the border.

A stern pursuit, a balcony scene, a cathedral, a duke changed, a secret of the king, and a thief in the night follow. Maria del Pilar comes to the rescue, with moonlight in the palace of the kings. The Williamsons mix motor touring, court intrigue, and love with their usual verve. Readers who like romantic adventure with a Spanish flavour will enjoy the car's winding road from puzzle to happy close.
24124-down-the-rhine-or-young-america-in:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, wrote this travel adventure for young readers, published in Boston in 1870. It is the sixth and last book of the first Young America Abroad series, closing the Academy Squadron's first voyage to Europe. The students and their friends leave their ships for an excursion into Germany.

The tale mixes sights, travel mishaps, and boyish adventure along the Rhine, meant to teach as well as amuse. Earlier books in the series had taken the same party through Ireland, England, Holland, France, and Switzerland. Readers get a brisk schoolboy tour of German towns, rivers, and roads in 1870.
2470-samuel-brohl-and-company:
Victor Cherbuliez's Samuel Brohl and Company follows a Jewish adventurer in Paris who reinvents himself as a count, chasing wealth and a wife among the high society he deceives. The novel's satire cuts both ways: Brohl's imposture exposes the snobbery of those he fools. Cherbuliez writes with a French novelist's polish and irony.

The book was a great success in its day, praised for its wit and its social observation. Its treatment of its hero now invites critical reading. Readers of French fiction will find a lively, provocative novel. Cherbuliez was a member of the French Academy and a popular novelist.
25880-american-poetry-1922-a-miscellany:
Printed by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1922, this miscellany gathers new American verse without tying it to one school or theme. A foreword recalls the stir caused by the first such volume in 1920, when readers kept asking who had edited a book that claimed no editor. The new book again refuses a single label, be it nature, love, patriotism, propaganda, or philosophy.

The table of contents runs from Amy Lowell, Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg, and Vachel Lindsay to James Oppenheim and Alfred Kreymborg, among others. Poems range from plain speech to bold experiment, with city voices, country voices, and a colophon that shouts its new America across plains and peaks. The set gives a wide, lively snap of verse in the early nineteen twenties.
26760-memories-of-bethany:
The Reverend John R. Macduff, author of Morning and Night Watches and Memories of Gennesaret, published these Bethany meditations with Robert Carter and Brothers at New York in 1861. Macduff inscribes them to mourners in Zion, for whom Bethany has always meant sorrow made holy.

Opening passages gather every Bethany reference in the sacred narrative. They run from Martha receiving Jesus into her house while Mary sits at his feet to Lazarus, sick at Bethany, dead four days, and raised. Martha meets Jesus on the road, confessing him as the Christ, the Son of God, while Mary sits still in the house. Chapters run from opening thoughts and the home scene through the messenger, the message, and the sleeper to the mourner's comfort, the mourner's creed, and the master.
27229-brother-bosch-an-airman-s-escape-f:
Captain Knight's Brother Bosch, an airman's escape from Germany, published by Heinemann in 1919, tells of capture and escape in the First World War. Dedicated to Captain Morritt, Lieutenant Medlicott, Lieutenant Walters, and all who gave their lives in the endeavour, it keeps the camp spelling Bosch for local colour.

Knight's fellow prisoners include Wolfe, commonly known as the Worm, and a second lieutenant forever on the prowl, never knocking before entering a room. The memoir moves from prison camp routine to the plans, risks, and luck of getting out, in a plain airman's voice.
27377-a-little-maid-of-massachusetts-col:
Alice Turner Curtis, author of A Little Maid of Province Town and A Little Maid of Narragansett Bay, wrote this girls' story of colonial Massachusetts. It was published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1915 with illustrations by Wuanita Smith. Its young heroine Anne lives among family, friends, and neighbors in the colony.

Chapters follow Amanda's mistake, Anne's decision, a visit with the Mashpees, and a stay at Brewster. They go on to a black-bearded man, a disappearance, a trip to Boston, a strange schooner, and a great adventure, ending homeward bound. Curtis mixes everyday colonial life with mild peril and friendship. Young readers get a gentle, old-fashioned historical tale.
2811-letters-of-pliny:
Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, known as Pliny the Younger, wrote these letters, here translated by William Melmoth and revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet. Born at Como in 62 AD, Pliny was eight when his father died, and he was adopted by his uncle, the elder Pliny, author of the Natural History.

The letters cover law, friendship, villas, and the eruption of Vesuvius, which killed his uncle. Pliny writes with polish, curiosity, and Roman civic pride. The collection remains a priceless window on imperial Rome, and a model of the familiar letter as literature.
28268-the-countess-of-albany:
Vernon Lee wrote The Countess of Albany in 1910, second edition, as a life of Louise, Countess of Albany, wife of Charles Edward Stuart, the Young Pretender. Lee, dedicating the book to a late friend, follows Louise from bride and bridegroom through Florence, Rome, and Colmar, to her salon and her final years at Santa Croce. Portraits illustrate the volume.

Chapters treat her escape, her separation, her years with Alfieri, and her circle of writers and artists. Lee writes with sympathy and care for sources. The biography suits readers of eighteenth-century history who want a woman's life at the centre of Jacobite romance.
28432-home-life-in-germany:
Mrs. Alfred Sidgwick's Home Life in Germany, first published in 1908, looks at German daily life from inside the home rather than from official reports. The author states plainly that she offers no statistics on taxes or building laws. She knows instead how German women spent their days.

Chapters cover children, schools, the education of the poor, girlhood, marriages, householders, housewives, servants, and town life. The result is a friendly, observant portrait of Germany before the First World War. It is valuable now as a record of customs, family routines, and attitudes that later histories rarely describe at close range.
29338-england-and-germany:
E. J. Dillon published this study of England and Germany in 1917, with an introduction by William Morris Hughes, prime minister of Australia. Dillon dedicates the book to Princess Alice of Monaco, calling it a partial presentment of the beginnings of a world cataclysm. Writing during the First World War, he seeks the roots of the conflict.

Chapters cover the character of Germany, its system of preparation, Italian finance, the annexation mania, Germany and Russia, and the statesmanship of the Entente. Later chapters treat Teuton politics, propaganda in Scandinavia, and the Balkans. Readers get a wartime analysis by a well-informed observer, partisan in tone but rich in the diplomacy and rivalries that led to war.
29934-the-auburndale-watch-company:
Edwin A. Battison, associate curator of mechanical and civil engineering at the Smithsonian's Museum of History and Technology, wrote this paper as number four in the museum's Contributions series. Its subtitle calls it the first American attempt toward the dollar watch. Battison based the study on the patent model of the Auburndale rotary and other company products in the National Museum, with other collections, including his own.

Five sections order the tale: The Invention, Developing the Invention, The New Sponsor, Success and Failure, and The Lesson. The dream was a machine-made watch with interchangeable parts, long in men's minds, crowned near Boston but missed at Auburndale. Careful digging brought to light the design and manufacturing errors behind the failure. The paper is a clear, short history of a bold, failed first try.
2995-tacitus-on-germany:
Tacitus wrote On Germany, in Thomas Gordon's translation, as a study of the Germanic peoples beyond Rome's frontier. Tacitus was probably born about 54 AD and died after 117, a friend of the younger Pliny, an advocate and orator, and the son-in-law of Agricola, conqueror of Britain. His short work describes tribes Rome knew mainly through war. The text records customs that struck Roman readers as strange.

Children were nourished with their own mothers' milk and never handed to nurses, and lords lived undistinguished from slaves, among the same cattle on the same ground. Free-born youths part from the rest when bravery recommends them. The Germania remains a key Roman source on northern Europe.
30386-the-one-and-the-many:
Milton Lesser tells The One and the Many, a short tale asking the one question: what lies beyond the ultimate? Some call the war foolish, and the narrator's brother said so in the Sunset Country. His brother, lame, does nothing but sketch star pictures, joining stars with lines as in a child's puzzle to make fish, archer, and hunter shapes. That, the narrator says, is foolish.

Perhaps it started it all, since he gazed at the stars hunting for pictures instead of minding his sentry post. Taken, with a hand from the darkness clamped over his mouth and a blade pricking the small of his back. He first feared the camp would be slain as it slept. The Onists, twenty archers against their outpost, had other ideas, and took him away on a night run through woodlands.
30464-a-manifest-destiny:
Julia Magruder writes A Manifest Destiny, illustrated and published in New York and London in 1900, following her earlier Magnificent Plebeian. Illustrations show Bettina throwing back her veil, sinking back in her chair, and hearing questions about a handsome boy, money partly her own, and the very spirit of widowhood.

Chapter one opens with Bettina Mowbray walking the deck of an ocean steamer bound for England, aware that many eyes watch her with interest. She studies their glances as closely as they study her, since being noticed by men and women of the world matters greatly to her. Magruder blends society romance with a heroine's keen sense of rank and reputation.
30798-sonny:
Rick Raphael wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in April 1963, about a hill boy in uniform and the strange power of a thought. Private Jediah Cromwell, new to the Army, feels homesick for the first time since he left the almost cut-off West Virginia hills of his birth. Back home, his mother Ma Cromwell feels trouble coming down the trail, in the shape of Cletus Miller, unseen since just before her husband died.

The tale links those two worlds, barracks and hollow, through a gift that seems to bend what thought alone can do. Raphael tells it in plain, folksy speech, with Jed's mother reading the hills as keenly as any scout. Readers get a short story about home, family, and a power no one can quite measure, told with warmth and a touch of mountain humor.
30871-legends-romances-of-brittany:
Lewis Spence, a fellow of the Royal Anthropological Institute, wrote this book of legends and romances of Brittany, published by Frederick A. Stokes in New York, with thirty-two pictures by W. Otway Cannell. Spence had already written Hero Tales and Legends of the Rhine, a dictionary of medieval romance, and myths of Mexico and Peru. His Brittany book moves from land and people to the old stones, fairies, and saints of the region.

Thirteen chapters treat menhirs and dolmens, fairies, sprites and demons, world-tales, Breton folk-tales, popular legends, hero-tales, the black art, Arthurian romance, the lays of Marie de France, saints, and costumes and customs. A glossary and index close the book. Pictures include Graelent and the fairy-woman, Merlin and Vivien, and fairies of Broceliande. It is a rich, old-fashioned guide to Breton lore.
31408-the-oxford-degree-ceremony:
J. Wells, a fellow of Wadham College, Oxford, wrote this short study of the Oxford degree ceremony, published by the Clarendon Press in 1906. Six chapters take the reader through the ceremony itself, its meaning, and its history, with attention to the forms, dress, and language that mark each stage. Wells writes as an insider explaining a ritual most visitors see only from outside.

The book's value lies in that explanation: it connects present practice to older custom and shows why each part of the ceremony survives. Students of Oxford, of academic ritual, or of English university life will find a clear, compact guide. It reads as both a handbook for the occasion and a small history of one of Oxford's most public traditions.
31737-the-sloths-of-kruvny:
Vern Fearing's short story was printed in Amazing Stories in October and November 1953. It is billed by its headnote as a very unserious yarn, offered because a sense of humor seems the only salvation in a grim world of atom bombs and worsening television commercials. Its hero is Bradley Broadshoulders, called Brad or Broad or Shoulders, an obese youth in the green tunic of the Galaxy Patrol.

Brad stands grim-lipped, as is the custom of spacemen, waiting for his commander, Metternich, known also as Foxey Gran'pa, to speak fateful words. Readers get a comic space story that sends up heroic postures, with a hero who has a tidy crop of Venusian fungus and no shred of muscle.
31922-felony:
James Causey's short story Felony, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in July 1954, follows a man named Vogel from childhood puzzles to man's greatest enigma. At nine, Vogel nearly killed another boy who scattered his half-finished jigsaw puzzle; at sixteen, the mysteries of the Danish Gambit moved him to tears.

At twenty-two, crouched in a foxhole on Okinawa, Vogel ignored death bursting about him to work on a tattered newspaper crossword. At thirty he managed production at Sachs Fixtures, tall, gaunt, and ruthless. Readers get a darkly comic tale of a pattern-seeking mind, for whom every system, from puzzles to crime, is a problem waiting to be solved.
32525-the-curlytops-at-uncle-frank-s-ran:
Howard R. Garis's Curlytops book, copyrighted in 1918, takes the Curlytops to Uncle Frank's ranch, subtitled Little Folks on Ponyback. Chapters open with Trouble's tumble, Nicknack and Trouble, off for the west, and a collision, followed by arrival at Ring Rosy Ranch and cowboy fun. Bad news, a queer noise, a sick pony, and a surprised doctor follow, with Trouble making a lasso.

Later chapters bring a bucking bronco, missing cattle, looking for Indians, Trouble helping, a trail, and the Curlytops alone. Julia Greene's illustrations accompany a story of ranch work, ponies, and family fun, in Garis's familiar series manner. Young readers get western adventure without harshness, as small children learn ranch manners and help, sometimes too eagerly, with real work.
32676-the-test-colony:
Winston Marks sends a test colony to Sirius XXII, a world reached after a dreary two-year voyage from Earth. Leader Phillip Benson and recorder Sam walk a sandy beach and meet two naked natives, male and female, who prove to be no stowaways from their own party.

The natives have four digits and no thumbs, long prehensile toes, and silky hair, and they watch the newcomers with frank curiosity. As contact grows, trade in a local fruit drink, broken quarantine rules, and a failure to check native births test Benson's plan to keep his colony from going native.
33052-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica gathers the entries running from Camorra to Cape Colony. Its articles include the Camorra, Campania and its Campagna, Tommaso Campanella, the Campbells from Alexander to Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, Cannae, Cannes, cannibalism, and Canning. Shorter entries on plants, places, and terms in the same alphabetical span sit alongside them. Transcriber's notes record corrections to articles on Canaan, cantata, and Cape Colony.

The slice mixes history, biography, geography, and natural science in the confident voice of early twentieth-century reference writing. Readers get the facts and judgments educated readers of the day were expected to trust, from a secret society to a colony's climate. As a reference text it is dated, but as a record of how knowledge was ordered a century ago, it remains a useful window on the period's mind.
34223-the-new-germany:
George Young's 1920 book The New Germany reports on Germany from the Armistice to the Treaty of Versailles. Young went to Berlin in January 1919 as a correspondent for the Daily News, and wrote most of the book in the summer of that year.

Seven chapters trace revolution, reaction, council republics, ruin and rebuilding, council rule, the treaty, and the new constitution. Young asks two plain questions: how far the German people had truly turned against Prussianism, and whether a lasting peace could be built on reform. Young adds an index, and his chapters run from the revolution to the new constitution in order.
4024-the-man-of-destiny:
A one-act play sets a young general at an inn during the Italian campaign, where a lady of rank and beauty enters with the poise of one used to privilege. Her flowered silk dress, Watteau pleat, and creamy fichu mark her station, while the innkeeper greets her with natural good manners.

Talk turns to dispatches, secrets, and the game of war, as the general finds his plans crossed by a woman as quick as he is. The play is a duel of wits in a single room, with history as its backdrop. Readers get a brisk, witty piece about power, charm, and the moment when a great man's fate hangs on a small exchange.
4349-wisdom-and-destiny:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote this essay on wisdom and destiny, translated by Alfred Sutro and dedicated to Georgette Leblanc. What began as a short piece of twenty pages, meant for a fortnight's work, grew over more than two years into a full volume. Maeterlinck calls it kin to his Treasure of the Humble, but different in treatment.

Where the earlier book speculated like a poet athirst for beauty, this one seeks truth like an earnest thinker. Maeterlinck asks how wisdom changes fate, and whether a life lived inwardly can meet outward chance. The essay suits readers of reflective prose who enjoy slow argument over quick advice.
4376-sowing-seeds-in-danny:
Nellie L. McClung wrote this Canadian novel about Mrs. Burton Francis, a dreamy woman with beautiful theories, and her silent husband. Camilla Rose, a capable young woman, looks after the household and sometimes helps apply those theories. The Watson family, including Pearl, an imaginative girl of twelve, works on the section and washes for the Francises.

McClung dedicates the story to her mother, with verses on kindness as what the old world needs. The novel tests Mrs. Francis's ideals against prairie life in Danny, where theory meets work, neighbors, and need. It is a warm, humorous book about good intentions, and about the people who must live with them.
6303-the-duel-between-france-and-germany:
Charles Sumner, speaking in Boston's Music Hall on October 26, 1870, calls the war then raging between France and Germany a duel, and draws its lesson for civilization. He takes classical warrant for the word, citing Livy on affairs settled by a pure and pious duel. Dryden's line adds that when kings make war, fortune is judge and soldiers are lawyers. The lecture asks what such a duel proves about nations.

Sumner traces the Spanish throne question, family ties binding an emperor's kinsman to France, and a French cabinet that chose its own ground for defiance. He argues that France was ready, and that readiness itself shaped the quarrel. This short lecture, reprinted from addresses on war, is a plea to judge war by reason and law, not by the field alone.
6580-charter-and-supplemental-charter-of:
King Charles the Second grants, in 1670, a royal charter to Prince Rupert and his partners for trade in Hudson's Bay. The text names dukes, earls, knights, and London merchants who paid for an expedition at their own great cost. It sets out their rights, lands, and powers in the formal, full language of a royal grant.

A later supplemental charter stands beside the first, adding to or shaping the company's legal frame. Together, the two texts form the legal root of a firm that shaped the fur trade and the map of northern North America. Readers here get the charters as they were written, not a retelling, with all their old titles and terms intact.
6814-the-curlytops-at-uncle-frank-s-ranc:
Howard Garis sends the Curlytops, Janet and Ted Martin, to Uncle Frank's ranch, or little folks on ponyback, at Ring Rosy Ranch. Trouble's tumble opens the fun, with Ted dressed in his father's coat and hat and spectacles too large for his nose, while Janet wears her mother's things. A collision, cowboy fun, bad news, and a queer noise follow.

A sick pony, a surprised doctor, a lasso, a bucking bronco, missing cattle, and a hidden valley test the children's pluck. Garis writes with bright, simple humor for young readers. The Curlytops at Uncle Frank's Ranch is a cheerful western for small children, full of ponies and play.
7238-my-four-years-in-germany:
James W. Gerard, late ambassador to the German imperial court, wrote My Four Years in Germany as a warning to his own people, and he puts that warning first as a foreword. He wants readers to grasp the gravity of the situation: German military and naval power, he insists, stood unbroken, and the twelve million men under arms could not be waved away.

Illustrations of court balls, safe conducts, and a special train of Americans leaving in August 1914 frame the memoir's insider view. Gerard dedicates the book to his wife, his small but tactful family of one, and his tone mixes diplomacy with plain alarm. The memoir reads as testimony from inside Berlin on the edge of war.
7465-richard-of-jamestown-a-story-of-the:
James Otis wrote this story to show children the home life of the colonists they meet in history books. His hero is Richard Mutton, whose name stands in the list of those sent to Virginia by the London Company on December 19, 1606. The story is told from a child's viewpoint, as if related by a child, so young readers meet Jamestown at their own eye level.

Otis deliberately avoids romance, dealing only with facts so far as possible. He describes daily life: the voyage, the settlement, and the hard work of conquering a wilderness for conscience or for gain. The book belongs to a series on colonial home life, and it still serves its purpose well: history as lived experience, not as a list of dates.
7499-through-five-republics-on-horseback:
G. Whitfield Ray, pioneer missionary and government explorer, rode through South America on horseback, and this book, in a revised twelfth edition of 1915, tells of those wanderings. The Reverend J. G. Brown of the Canadian Baptist missions introduces it. Ray's own preface quotes the Missionary Review of the World, which had called South America the darkest land, and claims that he penetrated part of its unexplored country.

The wanderings cross five republics, through regions where few outsiders had been. Ray writes as both missionary and explorer, noting peoples, rivers, and trails with a traveler's eye. An earlier editor, the book notes, abused it while admitting it sold like hot cakes. Readers bought it anyway, and had their eyes opened, as Ray intended.
8880-satanstoe-or-the-littlepage-manuscr:
James Fenimore Cooper writes Satanstoe, or the Littlepage Manuscripts. A tale of the colony, opening with Spenser's line that the only amaranthine flower on earth is virtue, and the only treasure, truth. His preface argues that every chronicle of manners has value, and double value when customs connect with principles in origin, development, or end. The Littlepage manuscripts, he says, show such a connection with important theories of Cooper's own time.

The novel follows the Littlepage family in colonial New York, through land, society, and the tensions that would become the anti-rent wars. Cooper, writing late in his career, uses a family chronicle to defend landed order and to criticize democratic excess as he saw it. Readers of American historical fiction will find a rich, if partisan, portrait of colonial life, and the first volume of a trilogy that runs into the early republic.
903-the-white-company:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this romance of the Hundred Years' War, about Alleyne Edricson, a young man who leaves his abbey. He joins the White Company, a band of English archers in France. Sir Nigel Loring leads them, and Samkin Aylward, the bowman, becomes Alleyne's friend and guide.

Doyle fills the tale with castles, battles, and chivalry, from the Pied Merlin inn to the fields of Spain. Alleyne grows from cloistered youth to tested man, learning honour, love, and war. The novel is a stirring, old-fashioned adventure, and a showcase for Doyle beyond Sherlock Holmes, rich in medieval colour.
a-century-too-soon-the-age-of-tyranny: John Roy Musick sets this romance a century too soon, in the age of tyranny after the Restoration in England. Historians, he notes, had paid little attention to that period in the American colonies, a hundred years before liberty was won. The story follows colonists whose hopes stir as the sleeping goddess of liberty seems to wake. Musick blends adventure and history in a tale of early resistance.
a-ryght-profytable-treatyse-compendiousl: Thomas Betson gathers writings of holy men into this short devotional treatise, printed at Caxton's house by Wynkyn de Worde around 1500. The tract was reprinted at Cambridge in 1905. It was one of twenty-six bound together in a volume given to the University in 1715 by King George the First, with the library of John Moore, Bishop of Ely. The author's name survives only from the colophon, read as Betson against an older reading of Betton.
brandes-main-currents-5-the-romantic-sch:
German Romantic writing fills the fifth book of Brandes's Main Currents, here in English. The Schlegels, Tieck, Novalis, and Hoffmann taught Europe new ways to dream and to doubt. Poetry, philosophy, and sly irony blend in their work.

Brandes traces how a circle of young talents remade German letters in a few bold years. He treats their longing for the infinite with sympathy and sharp insight. Fragments, fairy tales, and night pieces all find their place in his account. The volume shows why Romantic ideas from Germany spread so far across the whole of Europe.
brandes-main-currents-6-young-germany:
Young Germany closes Brandes's vast survey, in this sixth and final English book. Heine, Borne, and their allies turned writing into a weapon of politics. Literature left the study and entered the street fight for a freer Germany.

Brandes gives these radical voices his warmest praise and fullest energy. Wit, verse, and prose all serve one cause: breaking the grip of kings and censors. The survey ends where the modern age of engaged writing begins. Few works of criticism match the sweep of the full six books or their lasting sway over readers in many lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-flav:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Flavigny describes a Benedictine house in Dijon's diocese, founded in 721, the first year of Thierry the Fourth's reign, by Widerad, who richly endowed it. The Gallia Christiana places the new house, under St. Prix of Clermont, on an older monastic site from Clovis' time, once under St. Peter.

Pope John the Eighth dedicated the new church about 877, after which St. Peter's patronage prevailed definitively. Flavigny's fame rested partly on its relics and partly on its monks' piety, and the house stood at its height in the eighth century under Abbot Manasses. Manasses, authorised by Charlemagne to found Corbigny, brought St. Prix's relics from Volvic to Flavigny.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-pont: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Pontigny describes the second daughter of Cîteaux, on the Serain. Hildebert of Auxerre asked Cîteaux's St. Stephen for a monastery on a site he had chosen, and Stephen sent twelve monks in 1114 under Hugh of Mâcon. Their holy lives drew so many subjects that twenty-two monasteries arose in the first two abbots' lifetimes. Pontigny was known as a nursery of bishops and a refuge for great men, sheltering Canterbury archbishops Thomas, Stephen Langton and Edmund.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-savi:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Savigny describes a monastery on Normandy and Brittany's edge, founded by Vital de Mortain. Vital, a canon of St. Evroul, gave up his post for the hermit's life under Robert of Arbrissel, then withdrew to Savigny's forest in 1105 and built a hermitage.

Disciples soon gathered in such numbers that fit buildings rose, housing monks under St. Benedict's Rule, read much like the Cistercians' way. Rudolph, lord of Fougères, backed his grants in 1112, from which date the house counts its start. Savigny grew fast into one of France's most famed houses, and its founder and many later heads were made saints or blessed, St. Aymon best known among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albany:
The Diocese of Albany covers a wide stretch of eastern New York State, including the counties of Albany, Columbia, Saratoga, and Schenectady and parts of others, across 10,419 square miles. Of its 852,471 people, about 180,030 were Catholics, mostly of Irish, German, or French-Canadian origin. The entry traces the diocese from its colonial beginnings through its American growth.

Its sections follow the early missions and first parishes, such as St. Peter's at Troy in 1826 and St. John's at Schenectady in 1830. They then follow the bishops who built the diocese, including Francis McNeirny, consecrated in 1872. Later sections name the gifts that funded schools and churches and close with statistics for 1906. The clergy then numbered 214, among them Franciscans, Augustinians, Redemptorists, and Salesians, with teaching brothers in its schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-sax:
Albert of Saxony, also called Albert of Helmstädt, was a fourteenth-century philosopher nicknamed Albertus Parvus and Albertutius by the Italian scholastics. He passed his first examination at the University of Paris in 1351 and served as procurator and then rector of the university. He was still on its arts faculty in 1368, writing on Aristotle's work on the heavens and the world. He is often confused with a namesake who also taught at Paris.

All the works surviving under his name belong to Albert of Helmstädt, divided between logic and physics. Following his master Jean Buridan, he held that a projectile keeps moving because of an impetus, a push, put into it by the thrower. He likewise held that the heavens move by the impetus God gave them at creation. His favourite theory held earth and sea in balance, and his Treatise on Proportions went through eleven editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alimony:
Alimony, from Latin alimonia, nutriment, from alere, to nourish, is in common legal sense the court-ordered allowance a husband pays his wife living separately. It is also the allowance a former husband pays a divorced woman. Two kinds exist: alimony pendente lite, pending suit, and permanent alimony after suit. England's matrimonial jurisdiction once lay solely with ecclesiastical courts, which, despite common law making a wife's property her husband's on marriage, assigned separated wives part of his income.

Following canon law, those courts handled only separation suits, divorce a mensa et toro, and suits voiding marriage from the beginning. Pendente lite alimony could fall in either class, permanent alimony only in separation, since alimony, incidental to marriage, could not follow a void-from-the-beginning decree. A husband's non-payment exposed him to excommunication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
The Archconfraternity of the Holy Agony is an association honouring Christ's mental sufferings during his agony in the Garden of Gethsemane. Its object is to win, through those sufferings, peace for the church, defence of the faith, and an end to scourges, or afflictions. It also seeks a happy death for hardened sinners about to die, and spiritual aid for all in their death agony. It began as a confraternity in 1862 in Valfleury, France, founded by Antoine Nicolle, a Lazarist priest.

Pius IX enriched it with indulgences at the start. It was authorized in 1865 to affiliate other confraternities in the Lyons diocese. In 1873 it became an archconfraternity for all France, headquartered at the Lazarist mother house, 95 Rue de Sèvres, Paris. After two additions to its indulgences, Leo XIII in 1894 allowed its extension through the world. Joining requires only inscription on its register.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-cl:
Bernard of Cluny, a twelfth-century Benedictine poet and satirist, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth, homeland, and schooling are obscure, with claims for England, Morlaix in Brittany, and the Montpellier family all weighed. He is famed for his verses On the Contempt of the World, a long poem against the age's vices.

The poem does not march in order but eddies around two poles: the passing nature of earthly pleasure and the lasting joy of spiritual life. Vivid pictures of heaven and hell, in fierce and lofty diction, may have reached Dante. The entry presents a lyrical monk whose wrath and wonder still carry his verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethany:
Bethany, a village of Palestine, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Fifteen furlongs east of Jerusalem, at the foot of the Mount of Olives, it goes unmentioned in the Old Testament. The New Testament makes it shine as Mary, Martha, and Lazarus's village, where Jesus often found hospitality.

There Jesus raised Lazarus to life, the great miracle tied to the place, and near it he ascended into heaven. Its name most likely means house of misery, though the Talmud derives it from house of dates. The entry joins geography, etymology, and Gospel memory in one short piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calumny:
Calumny, from the Latin calvor, to use artifice or deceive, means in common use the unjust blackening of another's good name. It charges him with a crime or fault he did not commit. In general the sin is mortal, as detraction is, though it may be venial when the matter is trivial or deliberation lacking. Objectively it is mortal when it is meant to do serious harm to the person traduced.

Like one who wrongfully harms person or estate, the calumniator owes full reparation. He must retract his false words even at cost to his own name. He must also make good other losses his victim suffered, so far as he foresaw them. In canon law the oath of the parties to a suit, swearing good faith in bringing and defending the action, is called the oath of calumny.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceremony:
Ceremony in liturgy is an outward action, gesture, or movement that goes with the prayers and public worship of God. To these the Council of Trent adds the objects used in saying the prayers, such as blessings, lights, incense, and vestments. Ceremony answers to man's twofold nature, intellectual and sensible. As Aquinas says, man owes God a twofold adoration: spiritual in the inward devotion of the soul, and corporal in the outward form of worship.

Ceremonies serve several ends. They embellish and adorn sacred functions. They stir respect, devotion, and religion in the faithful. They lead the illiterate more easily to knowledge of the mysteries. They show the dispositions needed to receive the sacraments worthily, and move the faithful to keep their obligations with greater docility. The totality of a religion's rites is called its cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-huaul:
Charles Huault de Montmagny was the second French governor of Canada, born in France near the end of the sixteenth century and dead in the Antilles after 1651. Educated by the Jesuits, he joined the Order of Malta in 1622 and fought Muslims and African corsairs. Named to replace Champlain before the latter's death was even announced, he reached Quebec in June 1636. He rebuilt Fort St-Louis and laid out the city.

Under him rose the Jesuit College, the Ursuline monastery, and the Hôtel-Dieu of 1639. From the outset he pressed for converting the native peoples, and in 1636 the Sillery reduction began. When Maisonneuve arrived in autumn 1641 with forty colonists, Montmagny kept them and in spring escorted them personally to their goal. He also built Fort Richelieu, now Sorel, at the river's mouth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
George Cyprian Alston's entry covers the Congregation of Cluny, the earliest Benedictine reform to become practically a distinct order. It began at Cluny, northwest of Mâcon, where William the Pious, Duke of Aquitaine, founded an abbey in 910 and endowed it with his whole domain. He set Saint Berno of Gigny over it, launching a stricter Benedictine life. Benedict of Aniane's ideas from Aachen in 817 shaped the reform, whose chief departure was centralized government, foreign to Benedictine tradition.

The reform spread fast. For 250 years remarkable abbots ruled Cluny, marking Europe's history. After the twelfth century its power eased, and French wars harmed it sorely. Its abbey church ranked among the Middle Ages' wonders. Its library, for centuries among France's richest, stored vast manuscripts. Spirit and organization departed from tradition, yet monks stayed recognized as Benedictines. Alston draws on Bernard and Udalric of Cluny, Lorain, Champly, and Sackur.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-sax:
Stephen Donovan's entry follows Conrad of Saxony, also Saxo, Brunswick, or Holyinger. A Friar Minor and ascetical writer of uncertain birth, he died at Bologna in 1279. Holyinger is perhaps his family name. Some confuse him with another Conrad of Saxony who suffered for the Faith in 1284, but they were two distinct men, though of the same German province of the order. Conrad became provincial minister of Saxony in 1245 and ruled sixteen years with much zeal and prudence.

On his way to the 1279 general chapter, grievous illness struck him, and he died at Bologna that year. His writings include several sermons and the Speculum Beatae Mariae Virginis, at times wrongly attributed to Saint Bonaventure. The Friars Minor at Quaracchi recently edited the Speculum, and its preface sketches Conrad's life briefly while judging his other writings critically. Sources cite that Quaracchi edition of 1904 and the Analecta Franciscana volumes of 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-o-d:
The entry treats Cornelius O'Devany, Conchobhar O'Duibheannaigh, Bishop of Down and Connor, Ireland. Born about 1532, he died at Dublin in 1612, New Style. A Donegal Franciscan, he was appointed bishop in Rome in 1582, consecrated 2 February 1583. In 1588 he was committed to Dublin Castle. Failing to convict him of any capital crime, Fitzwilliam sought authority to be rid of him.

He escaped arrest until mid-1611, when, almost eighty, he was taken confirming and recommitted to Dublin Castle. On 28 January 1612 a packed jury found him guilty of treason, and he was sentenced to die on 1 February, Old Style. Drawn to the gallows past lamenting Catholics, he kissed the gallows, exhorted constancy, then was thrown off and quartered. Patrick O'Loughran, a priest arrested at Cork, suffered with him. The people carried off relics, prayed all night, and next night exhumed him for Saint James's Churchyard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmogony:
Cosmogony means an account of how the universe came to be, set against cosmology, the study of how the universe now works. Christian teaching answers with creation from nothing and providence guiding what followed. Modern science offers its own origin theories, while Genesis supplies the Mosaic account. This long entry surveys the ancient world's answers first.

Babylonian, Egyptian, Iranian, Indian, Phoenician, and Greek creation stories appear in turn, each quoted and weighed, before a summary draws their threads together. Norse and American origin tales close the survey. Readers meet gods rising from primeval waters, worlds shaped from chaos, and poets confessing that even heaven's seer may not know whence creation sprang.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
This reference entry follows a string of church councils held at Attigny, a royal residence near Vouziers in the Ardennes. It runs from the eighth century into the ninth. Meeting by meeting, it shows how bishops, kings, and popes used these assemblies to settle disputes, arrange penance, and discipline clergy and rulers alike.

Among the episodes it records are a 765 pact among bishops to pray and offer Masses for one another after death. At Charlemagne's 785 council, two conquered Saxon kings were baptized. In 822 Louis the Pious confessed his wrongs before bishops and Pope Paschal I. Later meetings judged a royal son accused of plotting against his father, and heard a bishop's appeal to Rome. The result is a compact chronicle of Frankish church politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphany:
Epiphany is the feast of Christ's manifestation, and this long entry traces its names, history, and customs. It was known as theophany, day of lights, day of washing, feast of the three kings, and Twelfth Day. Among Syrians it was called denho, or up-going, tied to the rising light of Luke's gospel.

The feast began in the Eastern Church. A homily of Hippolytus on baptism is sometimes linked to it, though its link is doubtful. The first sure reference is in Clement of Alexandria, who notes curious attempts to date Christ's birth to 20 May. Basilideans celebrated his baptism on 15 Tybi, or 11 Tybi by some accounts. From such Eastern roots the feast spread west, gathering the visit of the Magi, the baptism, and the wedding at Cana into one day of showing forth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-bauny:
Etienne Bauny, a theologian, was born in 1564 at Mouzon, Ardennes, France, and died on 3 December 1649 at Saint Pol de Léon. He entered the Society of Jesus on 20 July 1593. After teaching humanities and rhetoric, he rose to the chair of moral theology, which he held for sixteen years. For a time he was superior of the Jesuit residence at Pontoise.

Learning and holiness gave him a reputation that won the confidence of distinguished prelates. Cardinal de la Rochefoucauld chose him as spiritual director, and René de Rieux, Bishop of Léon, trusted him with his most delicate affairs. In moral theology he knew his subject profoundly, yet on many points he was too lenient. Jansenist anger at that leniency made him the target when Pascal and Arnauld charged the Jesuits with lax morality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-joseph-:
Franz Joseph Antony, born at Munster in Westphalia in 1790 and dead there in 1837, was a German church musician, choirmaster, and organist. Ordained priest, he became choirmaster at Munster Cathedral in 1819 and succeeded his father as organist in 1832. Besides songs he published four choral masses and two learned works that remain his monument. They are an archaeological and liturgical songbook of Gregorian chant in 1829, and a historical account of the origin and perfection of the organ in 1832.

The entry is short. But it places Antony among the nineteenth-century scholars who treated church music as history as well as art, tracing chant and organ building with erudition that later dictionaries of musicians still cite. His career, spent entirely in his native city, shows the quiet continuity of cathedral music, father to son at the organ loft.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germany:
Germany, a vast national history, traces the German people from tribal beginnings to the new empire. Its opening sets two clashing principles, German individualism against Rome's all-embracing authority. It follows Arminius's fight for freedom in the Teutoburg Forest into the Germanic states that grew from Rome's wreck. Theodoric dreamed of a Mediterranean confederation under the law of nations, yet Roman principle prevailed there while individualist forces prepared the national idea.

Only after Rome's western fall could a great Frankish kingdom gather the old Teutonic stock. Clovis overthrew Roman Gaul and built a Germano-Romanic state, colonizing conquered tribes in Roman fashion. Language, shifting consonants, and tribal shrines long divided rather than united the Germans. They lacked even a common name until theodisk, meaning popular, appeared in the ninth century. The survey runs on through medieval empire, Reformation, and unification to the new German empire, treating church and state throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gluttony:
Gluttony, from the Latin gluttire, to swallow or gulp down, is the excessive indulgence in food and drink. Its moral deformity lies in defying the order reason prescribes, which makes necessity the measure of eating and drinking. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sets out the five ways the Angelic Doctor names for this disorder.

The scholastic verse gives them as too soon, too expensively, too much, too eagerly, and too daintily. One who eats or drinks so as to injure health or unfit himself for his duties sins by gluttony. So does one who eats for mere pleasure alone. In general the sin is venial, but one who lives merely to eat and drink, whose god is his belly, or who gravely impairs his health, is guilty of mortal sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harmony:
Harmony, a concord of tones sounded together and the Greeks' general word for music, entered church chant only in the ninth century, though northern peoples may have sung in parts much earlier. The first added interval was a fourth below the melody, doubled at the octave to give a fifth above. Hucbald of St. Amand gave this organum its theory about 840 to 930.

Later centuries added contrary motion, the third as a consonance, the freely invented discant, and rules of counterpoint with measured notation, producing conductus, motet, and the perfected canon of the Netherland school. Through Palestrina's Roman school, melody still ruled and harmony followed its flow, resolving passing dissonance into rest, until the seventeenth century began to free individual feeling from the chant's diatonic reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-flavi:
Hugh of Flavigny was a Benedictine monk and historian, born about 1064, probably at Verdun, and dead before the middle of the twelfth century. Of a prominent family, he was schooled at St. Vannes in Verdun, where he took the novice's habit. When his abbot, a papal supporter, fled the emperor's bishop Dietrich and his antipope Clement III, Hugh followed him to St. Bénigne at Dijon.

At Dijon Hugh made his vows before Abbot Jarento, a strong friend of Gregory VII, and won the confidence of Jarento and of Archbishop Hugh of Lyons. In 1096, despite his youth, he was elected abbot of Flavigny. But disputes with the bishop of Autun and with his own monks, who would use even dishonest means for the pope, forced him twice to flee and finally to abdicate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-allarmet:
Jean Allarmet de Brogny, born at Brogny in Savoy in 1342 and dead at Rome in 1426, rose from herding swine to the cardinalate. Two monks, struck by the boy's ready answers, took him to Geneva and saw him schooled, finishing at Avignon. He then joined the Carthusians at Dijon, where his gifts soon drew notice.

Backed by the Avignon pope Clement VII, he became bishop of Viviers in 1380 and cardinal in 1385, later moving to Ostia-Velletri. At first he held the French obedience lawful, but by 1398 his orthodoxy turned him against it. He spent his later years working to end the schism that split the Western Church, a cause that shaped his whole public life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-levesque:
Jean Lévesque de Burigny, a French historian born at Reims in 1692 and dead in Paris in 1785. He began in 1713 with his brothers a twelve-folio manuscript dictionary of universal knowledge. At The Hague in 1718 he helped write Learned Europe in twelve volumes, contributing at least half.

Back in Paris, Burigny devoted himself to history and won rank as a careful scholar. Though sharing his age's philosophers' ideas, he was no extremist, but a modest, peace-loving man who wanted nothing beyond learning. His lives of Grotius and Erasmus hold facts found nowhere else, and his works range from papal authority and pagan theology to Sicily, Constantinople, Bossuet, and Du Perron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-alexan:
Joseph-Alexander Martigny was a French country priest who became a pioneer of Christian archaeology. Born at Sauverny in 1808, he taught at the little seminary of Belley, served parishes at Cressy, Arbignieu, and Bâgé-le-Châtel, and became an honorary canon in 1849. Encouraged by his bishop and by the scholar Abbé Greppo, he gave his spare hours to the study of early Christian remains.

His Dictionnaire des antiquités chrétiennes, published in 1865 and revised in 1877, was the first work of its kind, gathering varied articles all written by this learned village priest. Scholars in England and Germany soon took it up as a model, and Martigny also issued a French edition of De Rossi's archaeological bulletin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-sadoc-:
Joseph Sadoc Alemany was the first Archbishop of San Francisco. Born at Vich in Spain in 1814, he joined the Dominicans, was ordained at Viterbo in 1837, and spent ten years as a missionary in Ohio, Kentucky, and Tennessee, mastering English. Consecrated Bishop of Monterey in 1850, he moved to San Francisco as its first archbishop in 1853.

Alemany found only twenty-one adobe mission churches and a dozen priests in gold-rush California. He gathered priests and nuns, built churches and schools, and fought squatters and Mexico over church property and the Pious Fund. He resigned in 1884 and died in Spain in 1888, still a missionary at heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-friedric:
Karl Friedrich Savigny was a diplomatist born at Berlin in 1814 and dead at Frankfurt in 1875. He was the son of the jurist Friedrich Karl von Savigny and Kunigunde Brentano, the poet Clemens Brentano's sister. His father was Protestant and his mother Catholic, and the children followed their mother's faith. Schooled at Berlin, Rome, and Naples, he read law at Berlin, Munich, and Paris, entering Prussian service in 1836.

He served at London, Dresden, and Lisbon, then as ambassador at Karlsruhe, where Bismarck credited his tact with winning Baden for Prussia. In 1864 he moved to the Frankfurt Diet, where his 1866 reform motion, rejected on 14 June, brought Prussia's withdrawal and the Austro-Prussian War. With Bismarck he made peace with the southern states and helped frame the North German Confederation's constitution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litany:
A litany is a form of prayer in which a leader speaks short petitions. The people answer each one, often with Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy. The entry roots the pattern in Psalm 136, where every verse ends with a repeated refrain. It also points to the song of the three youths in Daniel.

Eastern Masses, the Milan rite, and the Roman Missal all keep litanies. They range from Good Friday prayers for every class of people to the triple Kyrie of each Mass. The entry shows how one simple device, a spoken need met by a shared answer, grew into public worship, private devotion, and prayers for times of trouble.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludolph-of-sa:
Ludolph of Saxony, called Ludolph the Carthusian, was a fourteenth-century devotional writer, dead on 13 April 1378. His birthplace is unsure, despite his name, and he may have come from Cologne or Mainz dioceses, then in Saxony province.

After thirty years as a Dominican, steeped, it may be, in Tauler and Suso, he entered the Strasbourg Charterhouse about 1340, governed the new Coblenz house, then resigned from scruple in 1348. His last thirty years passed in retreat at Mainz and Strasbourg. His Psalm commentary, popular across Germany, and his Vita Christi, a meditation on Christ's life rather than a plain biography, commend him still, though he never won public cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orders-of-sai:
Orders of Saint Anthony gather the many communities claiming Anthony the Hermit, father of monasticism, as patron or rule-giver. Disciples flocked to his Thebaid hermitage, some 6,000 by Rufinus's count, living apart or together under his word and example alone.

A rule drawn from Anthony's letters later shaped Eastern houses, though their actual rules reach only to Basil. Maronite Antonians split into Saint Isaiah and Saint Eliseus congregations, approved in 1740 and 1732, while Hospital Brothers of Saint Anthony, founded about 1095, nursed victims of Saint Anthony's fire. A rule under Anthony’s name was drawn from his letters and precepts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pardons-of-br:
Pardons of Brittany are the feasts of a church or chapel's patron saint, at which an indulgence is granted. Pardon comes from Latin perdonare, to forgive, shading through old French forms toward a gift. The pardons reach no farther east than Guingamp, whose feast falls on the first Sunday in July. They run from March to October, mostly between Easter and Michaelmas.

Five pardons stand out by kind. Saint Yves at Treguier is the pardon of the poor. Our Lady of Rumengol is the pardon of singers. Saint Jean-du-Doigt is the pardon of fire. Saint Ronan is the pardon of the mountain. Saint Anne de la Palude is the pardon of the sea. Largest crowds gather at Saint Jean-du-Doigt on 24 June and Saint Anne d'Auray on 24 July, the latter Brittany's most famous pilgrimage, with each parish known by its costume.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-pazmany:
Peter Pázmány was the Hungarian cardinal who turned his country back toward Catholicism, dying in 1637. Born of Calvinist parents, he was drawn to the Church by his Catholic stepmother and Jesuit teachers, converted at thirteen, and entered the Jesuit novitiate at seventeen. After four years under Bellarmine at Rome, he taught at Graz, then rose through Turóc and Nyitra to Archbishop of Esztergom in 1616 and Cardinal Primate.

His pen fought Stephen Magyary's charge that Catholicism ruined Hungary, and his Hodoegus of 1613, part dogma and part polemic, argued the Catholic case unanswerably. He translated the Imitation of Christ, built seminaries and a college at Nagyszombat, and founded Hungary's first university there in 1635. As statesman he backed Ferdinand II and made peace with Bethlen in 1622. He was born in Protestant Hungary and died in a Catholic one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxony:
Saxony, in this entry, means first the Saxon tribe and then the land and kingdom that took its name. In third- and fourth-century Germany great tribal confederations replaced many small tribes: Alamanni, Bavarians, Thuringians, Franks, Frisians, and Saxons. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a people from sea raiders to a modern kingdom.

Unlike the other confederations, ruled by kings, Saxons lived in independent bodies under chiefs, electing a duke only in war. At first a small tribe between the Elbe and Eider in Holstein, they took their name, it seems, from the sax, a stone knife. They fought westward until their name covered a confederation reaching almost to the Rhine. The entry then traces Saxon conversion, duchies, and the kingdom's church history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scrutiny:
Scrutiny, Latin scrutinium from scrutari, to search or investigate, is a term used in several ways in canon law. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia begins with promotion to orders, where candidates must be examined, following Paul's warning not to lay hands hastily on any man. That practice is ancient, witnessed by Cyprian, who died in 258, in his thirty-eighth letter.

The ninth canon of Nicaea in 325 already assumes scrutiny of candidates in use, and many later synods enforced and defined it more exactly. Trent's discipline, in session twenty-three, chapter five on reform, orders a threefold scrutiny. First comes inquiry into the candidate's qualities by parish priest and teachers and by public proclamation in church, embodied in a testimonial letter to the bishop. A second scrutiny follows shortly before ordination through the bishop's own examination.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sejny:
Sejny, a diocese in the northwest of Russian Poland near East Prussia, began as the see of Wigry. Pius VI carved it out in 1798 from the diocese of Vilna after the first partition of Poland. This entry traces its seat at the Camaldolese monastery of Wigry, founded under King Jagiello in 1418. Its first bishop was the celebrated preacher Michael Francis Karpowicz. His successor, John Clement Golaszewski, enlarged the Wigry cathedral.

After the third partition gave the land to Russia, Pius VII reorganized the Polish church in 1818. He moved the see to Augustów, a city founded in 1561 by Sigismund Augustus. Its new cathedral opened that December. The entry closes with later bishops and the slow decline of monastic life under Russian rules against receiving novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simony:
Simony, named from Simon Magus in Acts chapter 8, is usually defined as a deliberate plan to buy or sell for a temporal price things spiritual or joined to spiritual things. Any exchange of spiritual for temporal goods counts, even where a motive of gain suffices without a formal price. Temporal advantages fall into three classes: gain by hand, meaning money and property; gain by tongue, meaning praise and support in high places; and gain by service, meaning undue homage.

Spiritual objects cover whatever serves the soul's eternal welfare, from grace and sacraments to sacramentals. The entry sorts borderline cases with care. A Mass stipend for the celebrant's support is lawful, but payment for the Mass itself is sinful. Chancery fees for dispensations are allowed, but payment for jurisdiction is not. Penalties close the article, from void benefices to excommunication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anthony:
St. Anthony was the founder of Christian monasticism, and this entry weighs the sources for his life with care. Its chief source is a Greek Life attributed to St. Athanasius, found in any edition of his works. Scholars now receive it with practical unanimity as a substantially historical record. They also judge it probably an authentic work of Athanasius.

Valuable supporting material comes from the Apophthegmata, chiefly sayings collected under Anthony's name, and from Cassian and Palladius. All that material may probably be accepted as substantially authentic. What Jerome's Life of St. Paul the Hermit relates about Anthony, by contrast, cannot be used for historical purposes. The entry gives readers both the hermit's story and the scholarship that tests it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lazarus-of:
Lazarus of Bethany, reputed first bishop of Marseilles, reaches Provence in the entry through a miraculous sea voyage. Tradition, combined across epochs, says Bethany's family, friends of Christ, with holy women and other disciples, were set adrift by Jews hostile to Christianity in a vessel lacking sails, oars, or helm. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places their landing at the Saintes-Maries.

There the company scattered to preach across southeastern Gaul. Lazarus went to Marseilles, converted many inhabitants, and became their first pastor. Under Nero's first persecution he hid in a crypt, over which St.-Victor's abbey rose in the fifth century, and there he was buried after shedding blood for the faith. Under Domitian he was imprisoned and beheaded at a spot still believed to mark the place. The entry calls the whole a series of traditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vitalis-of:
Vitalis of Savigny, founder of Savigny's monastery and congregation in 1112, preached to outcasts from a hermit's forest life. Born at Tierceville near Bayeux about 1060 to 1065 to Rainfred and Rohais, he became after ordination chaplain to Robert of Mortain, the Conqueror's brother. Robert gave him a canonry at St Evroult in Mortain, founded in 1082.

Longing for a more perfect life, Vitalis gave up the canonry in 1095, settled at Dompierre nineteen miles east of Mortain, and joined the hermit colony of the forest of Craon. For seventeen years he lived ascetically, preaching with zeal, fearless speech, and tireless energy. He helped the outcasts gathering round him and reportedly tried to reconcile Henry I with Robert Curthose. He died at Savigny on 16 September 1122.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tuscany:
Tuscany is the central Italian region that matches the old land of Etruria. It takes in the provinces around Florence, Pisa, Siena, Arezzo, Grosseto, Livorno, and Massa. The entry gives its size and its population of nearly three million in 1911. It also sets out its church geography, with archdioceses at Florence, Pisa, and Siena and a string of smaller sees. Its story runs from Etruscan dominance and Roman conquest through medieval communes and feuding cities.

The narrative follows Florence's rise under the Medici, from bankers and republican rulers to hereditary dukes and then grand dukes of the whole region. It covers Cosimo I and his firm ordering of the state, the splendour and decay of his successors, and the later rule of the house of Lorraine. It ends with the region joining the new Kingdom of Italy in the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-cha:
Charles Mahony was an Irish Franciscan priest executed at Ruthin in North Wales in August 1679. Born after 1639, he is known chiefly from a single printed sheet recording the last speeches of three priests executed that year, supplemented by Bishop Challoner's account. Mahony was seized while travelling to his native Ireland, driven by sea onto the Welsh coast.

At his trial at Denbigh he confessed himself a priest and was condemned, though, as his speech protested, he had never exercised his ministry in England before his capture. He forgave his judges, prayed for the king, and asked God to convert him to the Catholic faith. He suffered in his Franciscan habit, with great constancy, cut down alive and butchered according to sentence, as Challoner recalled from a manuscript he could no longer recover.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Northern Germany, or the Northern Missions, is a vicariate covering Mecklenburg, Schaumburg-Lippe, the Hanse towns Hamburg, Lübeck. Bremen, the Oldenburg principality of Lübeck, and Helgoland, under the permanent administration of the Bishop of Osnabrück. The wider missions also include the prefecture of Schleswig-Holstein, placed under a separate prelate in 1868.

Catholics numbered about 79,400 among nearly two million others, served by forty-seven secular priests in seventeen parishes and seventeen mission stations. With houses of Sisters of Mercy, Grey Nuns, Franciscan sisters, and Ursulines. Schleswig-Holstein added 35,900 Catholics in eleven parishes and thirty-one stations. In summer the flock swelled by 17,000 to 20,000 labourers, chiefly Poles, who returned home at winter's start.
charter-and-supplemental-charter-of-the-:
The Charter and Supplemental Charter of the Hudson's Bay Company prints the royal documents that created one of history's great trading firms. The original charter, granted by Charles the Second in 1670, names Prince Rupert and a company of London merchants and gentlemen as the body corporate.

Its purpose was an expedition to Hudson's Bay in north-west America, seeking a new passage to the South Sea and trade in furs, minerals and other commodities. The adventurers bore the whole cost themselves, and the charter gave their company governing rights over the lands and waters it entered. The supplemental charter that follows extends and confirms those powers. Readers of Canadian and commercial history will find here the legal root of a company that shaped a continent's fur trade.
frank-and-fanny:
Moore, writing as Mrs. Clara Moreton, tells a quiet rural story for the young. Her preface rejects exciting narratives and hairbreadth escapes on purpose. Gentleness, patience, and benevolence are the virtues she means to grow, through simple scenes of country life.

The schoolyard supplies the story's small cruelty. Jack Mills pins a taunting paper on Fanny's back and shouts names after the pair. When Fanny stoops to pick a flower, Jack's thrown stone strikes her face and draws blood. Frank's first impulse is pursuit, but he stays to learn how badly his sister is hurt. The book appeared at Boston in 1851.
